title: Tailoring CVs & ATS basics
summary: Tailor your CV to each role and get past the Applicant Tracking System by mirroring keywords and using clean, parseable formatting.
objectives: Understand what an Applicant Tracking System (ATS) does and why it matters
Read a job description and extract the keywords that matter
Tailor your CV to each role without lying or stuffing
Use a clean, single-column, parseable CV layout
Write achievement bullets using the action-metric-result formula
Position a maths background and L1 support internship for AI roles
Avoid common formatting traps that break ATS parsing

quiz.q: What does an ATS primarily do with your CV?
options: Reads it like a human recruiter
Parses it into structured fields and scores it against the job
quiz.why: An ATS parses your CV into fields (skills, experience, education) and ranks it against the job's keywords before a human ever sees it.

quiz.q: Which CV format is safest for ATS parsing?
options: A two-column PDF with text boxes
A simple single-column document with standard headings
quiz.why: Single-column text with standard headings (Experience, Education, Skills) parses cleanly; columns, text boxes, and images often scramble or get dropped.

quiz.q: What is the best source for the keywords you should put in your CV?
options: The specific job description you are applying to
quiz.why: Each job description names the exact skills and tools the employer screens for; mirror that role's language rather than a generic list.

quiz.q: Why is keyword stuffing (repeating terms unnaturally) a bad idea?
quiz.answer: It reads as spam to humans, can be flagged, and does not demonstrate real evidence of the skill.
quiz.why: Modern ATS and recruiters look for context and evidence; cramming keywords without achievements fails the human review even if it passes parsing.

quiz.q: Give one strong way to phrase a CV achievement bullet.
quiz.answer: Use action verb + what you did + measurable result, e.g. 'Automated weekly ticket report with Python, cutting manual work by 3 hours.'
quiz.why: The action-metric-result formula turns vague duties into evidence and naturally includes role keywords.

quiz.q: How many distinct CV versions should you ideally keep?
options: A master CV plus a tailored version per role
A new CV written from scratch each time
quiz.why: Keep one master CV with everything, then cut and reorder it into a tailored version for each role — fast and consistent.

body_markdown:
## What an ATS actually is

An **Applicant Tracking System (ATS)** is software employers use to collect, parse, and rank job applications. When you upload a CV, the ATS does not read it like a person — it tries to extract structured fields (your name, jobs, dates, skills, education) and then scores how well those fields match the job description.

If your CV is hard to parse, key information gets lost or jumbled before a human ever sees it. So step one is simply: **be parseable**.

## Mirror the job description

Every job description is a free answer key. It tells you the exact tools, skills, and phrases the employer screens for. Your job is to **mirror that language honestly** — if you genuinely have the skill, use the same word the employer used (say "Python" not just "scripting", "SQL" not just "databases").

A quick trick: paste the job description into a script and pull out the most frequent meaningful words.

```python
import re
from collections import Counter

jd = open("job_description.txt", encoding="utf-8").read().lower()
words = re.findall(r"[a-z][a-z+#.]+", jd)
stop = {"and", "the", "with", "you", "for", "our", "to", "of", "in", "a"}
common = [w for w in words if w not in stop and len(w) > 2]

for word, n in Counter(common).most_common(20):
    print(f"{n:>3}  {word}")
```

Then make sure the genuine matches appear in your CV — ideally in a **Skills** section and again as **evidence** inside an achievement bullet.

## Keep the format clean

Fancy layouts break ATS parsing. Two-column designs, text boxes, tables, images, and headers/footers often get scrambled or dropped. Use a **single-column** layout, standard section headings, and a normal font.

Write your CV in a plain format you control, like Markdown, then export to PDF:

```bash
# Convert a clean markdown CV to PDF with pandoc
pandoc cv.md -o cv.pdf --pdf-engine=xelatex
```

Use standard headings the ATS expects: **Experience**, **Education**, **Skills**, **Projects**. Save the file with your name, e.g. `Dami-Adeyemi-CV.pdf`.

## Write achievement bullets, not duties

Don't list what you were *responsible for* — show what you *achieved*. Use the formula **action verb + what you did + measurable result**.

- Weak: "Responsible for handling support tickets."
- Strong: "Resolved 40+ L1 support tickets per week, automating the weekly report in Python and saving 3 hours."

The strong version naturally includes keywords (Python, support) and gives evidence a number proves.

## Position your maths + support story

You are not "just" a maths graduate with a support internship — that's a strong, in-demand combination. Maths signals **statistics, linear algebra, and rigour**; L1 support signals **debugging, communication, and working under pressure**. Frame projects (your course work) as a **Projects** section so a thin work history still shows real, applied AI skills.

## Your task

Take one real job advert, extract its keywords, and produce a **tailored** single-column CV with at least three achievement bullets in the action-metric-result format.

slides.title: Tailoring CVs & ATS basics
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Six, where we turn all your hard work into job offers. In this lesson we'll cover how to tailor your C V to each role and get past the Applicant Tracking System, often shortened to A T S. By the end you'll know how the software reads your C V, how to mirror a job description, and how to write bullets that prove you can do the work.

slides.title: What is an ATS?
bullets: Software that collects and ranks applications.
It parses your CV into structured fields.
It scores you before a human sees it.
Step one: be easy to parse.
slides.narration: Let's start with what an A T S actually is. It's software employers use to collect and sort job applications. When you upload your C V, the system doesn't read it like a person. Instead it tries to pull out structured fields, like your jobs, dates, and skills, and then scores how well they match the role. So the very first rule is simple: make your C V easy for the machine to parse.

slides.title: The job description is your key
bullets: Every advert lists the exact skills wanted.
Mirror that language honestly.
Say Python, not just scripting.
Match the role, not a generic list.
slides.narration: Here's the good news: every job description is a free answer key. It names the exact tools and skills the employer screens for. Your job is to mirror that language honestly. If the advert says Python and S Q L, and you genuinely have those skills, use those exact words rather than vague ones like scripting or databases. Always tailor to the specific role, never a generic list.

slides.title: Extract keywords fast
bullets: Paste the advert into a script.
Count the most frequent meaningful words.
Cross-check against your real skills.
slides.code:
import re
from collections import Counter

jd = open("job.txt").read().lower()
words = re.findall(r"[a-z][a-z+#.]+", jd)
for w, n in Counter(words).most_common(15):
    print(n, w)
slides.narration: You can speed this up with a tiny Python script. Read the job description, lowercase it, split it into words, and count the most frequent ones. The top results show you the language the employer cares about. Then cross-check that list against the skills you genuinely have, and make sure those matches appear on your C V.

slides.title: Keep the format clean
bullets: Single column, standard headings.
No tables, text boxes, or images.
Normal font, no header or footer tricks.
Headings: Experience, Education, Skills.
slides.narration: Fancy layouts are where most people lose. Two-column designs, text boxes, tables, and images often get scrambled or dropped when the A T S parses them. Stick to a single column with standard headings like Experience, Education, and Skills. Use a normal font and avoid putting key details in headers or footers, because parsers frequently ignore those.

slides.title: Write it in plain text
bullets: Author in Markdown you control.
Export to a clean PDF.
Name the file with your name.
slides.code:
# Markdown to PDF
pandoc cv.md -o cv.pdf \
  --pdf-engine=xelatex

# Result: Dami-Adeyemi-CV.pdf
slides.narration: A reliable trick is to write your C V in a plain format you fully control, like Markdown, then export it to P D F. Tools like pandoc do this in one command. The output is a clean, parseable P D F with no hidden formatting traps. Finally, name the file with your own name so a busy recruiter can find it instantly.

slides.title: Bullets: action, metric, result
bullets: Show achievements, not duties.
Action verb plus what plus a number.
Numbers turn claims into evidence.
slides.code:
Weak:
  Responsible for support tickets.

Strong:
  Resolved 40+ tickets/week,
  automating the report in Python,
  saving 3 hours.
slides.narration: Now the heart of a great C V: the bullets. Don't list what you were responsible for; show what you achieved. Use the formula action verb, what you did, and a measurable result. Compare responsible for support tickets with resolved forty plus tickets a week and automated the report in Python, saving three hours. The strong version proves the skill with a number and naturally includes keywords.

slides.title: Your maths + support story
bullets: Maths signals stats, algebra, rigour.
L1 support signals debugging and comms.
Use a Projects section for course work.
A thin history can still look strong.
slides.narration: Don't undersell your background. A maths degree signals statistics, linear algebra, and genuine rigour, which A I teams want. Your L one support internship signals debugging, clear communication, and grace under pressure. And because your work history is still short, add a Projects section showing the applied A I work from this course. Together, that's a compelling, in-demand story.

slides.title: Honesty and one master CV
bullets: Never lie or stuff keywords.
Stuffing fails the human review anyway.
Keep one master CV with everything.
Cut it down per role.
slides.narration: Two final principles. First, be honest. Stuffing keywords you can't back up might pass the parser, but it fails the moment a human reads it, and lying can cost you the offer. Second, keep one master C V that contains everything you've ever done, then cut and reorder it into a tailored version for each role. That's fast, consistent, and keeps every application sharp.

Keep a clean single-column format. And write bullets using the action, metric, result formula to prove your skills.
